profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a UK financial services law firm advising a trade association of digital lending platforms on a proposed voluntary compliance framework for AI-assisted credit decisions. The framework is intended to operate as a soft-law instrument: a non-binding code of practice that members can adopt ahead of likely FCA scrutiny and possible future statutory reform. The agenda is to review the near-final draft of the framework, especially its sections on governance, explainability, customer communications, internal monitoring, and regulator engagement, and decide whether it is ready to circulate to the association board next week. The expected outcome is agreement on whether the draft is 'board-ready' and what limited revisions should be made before circulation.

members.name: Amira Shah
members.expertise: UK conduct regulation, FCA supervisory engagement, industry codes, regulatory strategy
members.background: Amira has spent fifteen years advising banks, fintechs, and trade bodies on conduct risk and non-statutory regulatory frameworks; she previously worked in the FCA's supervision division and now leads the firm's soft-law and market standards practice.
members.private_state: She wants the framework to look credible and mature enough to reassure the association board and invite constructive FCA engagement without creating quasi-binding obligations that members will refuse to sign up to.
hidden_assumptions: A 'principles-based' code should preserve discretion for firms and avoid highly operational commitments that could later be treated as a de facto rulebook.
If the draft is 'board-ready,' it means the structure and risk posture are settled, even if examples, annexes, and implementation mechanics are still to be polished afterward.
The section on 'monitoring' is about periodic governance oversight and exception escalation at committee level, not file-level testing of individual lending outcomes.

References to the 'regulator' in this project are primarily about future informal engagement with the FCA policy and supervision teams, not obtaining advance comfort from every potentially interested authority.

members.name: Daniel Mercer
members.role: Senior Knowledge Counsel, Public Law and Consumer Finance
members.expertise: administrative law, consumer credit, drafting compliance frameworks, governance documentation
members.background: Daniel previously worked in-house at a consumer finance group designing internal governance standards and now supports cross-practice drafting projects, translating high-level legal positions into operational review criteria and implementation text.
members.private_state: He wants the framework to be sufficiently concrete that member firms can actually implement it consistently and point to it as evidence of serious consumer-protection discipline if challenged later.
hidden_assumptions: A 'principles-based' code still needs enough operational specificity that different firms would apply it in broadly the same way under scrutiny.
If the draft is 'board-ready,' it means the board could approve circulation to members without expecting material annexes, decision logs, or implementation details to be added later.
The section on 'monitoring' should include sample-based outcome testing and documented review of declined and borderline credit decisions, because governance without evidential testing is weak.
The plan already assumes at least some pre-circulation sounding with the FCA innovation or supervision contacts because the framework is being positioned as anticipatory good practice.
When a draft says 'customer communication,' it should include not only external notices to applicants but also the model wording and trigger logic firms will use in adverse action explanations.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the draft is 'board-ready' for next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amira means the core architecture, legal posture, and strategic positioning are sufficiently settled for the association board to review, even if implementation annexes and examples are added afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel means the package is complete enough that the board could approve release without expecting substantive supporting materials still to be written.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In law-firm design reviews, 'board-ready' routinely sounds like a shared maturity threshold, and both participants are competent enough that neither expects the other to be using a materially different completeness standard.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the framework needs a stronger 'monitoring' section.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amira treats monitoring as governance-layer review: quarterly committee oversight, MI dashboards, issue escalation, and responsibility allocation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel treats monitoring as including operational testing: sampling declined applications, checking explanations, and reviewing outcome patterns for bias or inconsistency.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both governance oversight and testing are normal subcomponents of compliance work, so the umbrella term 'monitoring' creates a natural but false sense that they are discussing the same package of activities.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'socialising it with the regulator' before or after board circulation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amira presupposes this means optional, informal post-board engagement with FCA policy or supervision contacts to show the sector is acting responsibly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel presupposes there is already an expectation of some pre-circulation external sounding, likely with existing FCA contacts, to test whether the proposed wording on explainability and customer outcomes lands safely.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both treat regulator engagement as ordinary background process rather than a headline decision, so each assumes timing and purpose were implicitly settled in earlier project conversations.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the draft should be clearer on 'customer communication'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amira means the public-facing statement of principles and broad customer-facing explanation commitments that member firms can adapt.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel means the actual adverse-action wording framework, trigger points, and minimum explanation content to be used in applicant communications.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In consumer-finance legal drafting, 'customer communication' can naturally refer either to strategic disclosure principles or to operative notice text, and both uses are common enough that neither speaker hears a red flag.

turns.inner_thought: I want this framed as a near-final strategic review, not an invitation to reopen the whole instrument. If the architecture, tone, and risk posture are settled, then it is board-ready for next week. The board does not need every annex, worked example, or implementation note finished before seeing it; those can follow once they bless the direction.
turns.utterance: Thanks, Daniel. I thought we could use this as the final design review of the code before we decide whether it's board-ready for the association meeting next week. From my side, the core structure is there; I mainly want to make sure the last bits are landing in the right tone.

turns.inner_thought: It is strong overall, but I need to make sure we are not sending something up as board-ready if the board would still expect substantive annexes, decision logs, or implementation detail to be written later. In my mind, board-ready means they could approve circulation without us still building key supporting materials afterward.
turns.utterance: Yes, broadly I think it's in good shape. What I want to pressure-test today is whether the package is genuinely board-ready, in the sense that it can go up cleanly without the board feeling there are still supporting pieces missing.

turns.inner_thought: The biggest risk is drift into quasi-rules. Members will resist if this starts to read like a covert supervisory manual. The code needs enough substance to reassure the association board and later the FCA, but it must preserve discretion and stay recognisably principles-based.
turns.utterance: I agree. My main instinct is still that we keep the drafting firmly principles-based. The association wants something credible and mature, but if it starts reading like a disguised rulebook we'll lose people very quickly.

turns.inner_thought: Principles-based is fine, but not at the expense of consistent application. Right now the monitoring section feels too high-level. Firms need to know what evidence they should be able to show if challenged, and that includes actual testing rather than just governance rhetoric.
turns.utterance: I think that's right, and I don't see a conflict with making one or two areas a bit tighter. The place that still feels light to me is monitoring. We say the right things, but I think the framework needs a stronger monitoring section so firms are clearer on what they should be able to evidence.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, monitoring can be strengthened, but at governance level: committee cadence, MI, escalation, ownership. I do not want to write in anything that looks like mandatory case testing or fixed review mechanics, because that is exactly how a voluntary code hardens into a de facto rulebook.
turns.utterance: I'm comfortable with that. We can strengthen monitoring through clearer committee review language, better use of management information, and a more explicit escalation route where something looks off. That would give the section a bit more backbone without overloading it.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I also want to get in the operational part without making a speech about it. A short paragraph should do it: monitoring declined and borderline cases, and checking that the explanation actually matches the decision basis. That ties monitoring to customer communication in a practical way.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I also wondered about adding a short paragraph under monitoring that deals with declined and borderline cases, and making sure there is a check that the explanation given to customers lines up with the basis of the decision.

turns.inner_thought: Fine as long as it still reads at a high level. For me the customer communication point is there to show the board the code supports a coherent outward narrative on transparency and fairness, not to lock firms into scripted notices or trigger mechanics. If Daniel tidies that messaging, it helps the board story.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that lands well. On customer communication more generally, I'd like the section to show the board quite clearly that the code gives members a sensible external narrative around transparency and fairness.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed. I can sharpen customer communication by setting clearer minimum content for adverse outcome explanations and when that wording is used. That is exactly the sort of thing firms need if this is meant to be implemented consistently and later relied on as evidence of discipline.
turns.utterance: Understood. I can refine the customer communication piece so the minimum content is a bit sharper around how firms explain adverse outcomes and when that wording is used.

turns.inner_thought: Assuming those tweaks are made, the obvious next step is board first, then socialising it with the regulator afterward on an informal basis with FCA policy or supervision contacts. I don't want us looking as though we're seeking pre-clearance from every authority before the association board has even seen its own framework.
turns.utterance: Good. Then the other question is timing: once those refinements are in, are we comfortable socialising it with the regulator after the board has seen it?

turns.inner_thought: Yes, though in my mind that conversation is part of the near-term process and the text needs to be robust enough for pre-circulation sounding with FCA contacts if needed. They will expect to see a workable governance and testing model, not just aspiration, so I should draft with that in mind.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. I'll make sure the text is in good shape for that conversation, because I think the regulator will want to see a workable governance and testing model rather than something purely directional.

turns.inner_thought: That all sounds manageable. To me these are light revisions, not substantive blockers. Once the monitoring and customer communication wording is cleaned up, the draft is board-ready and we can let the association board focus on strategic comfort rather than drafting detail.
turns.utterance: Fine. In that case, I think we're really talking about light revisions rather than any structural rethink. If we clean up the monitoring and customer communication wording, I would be comfortable saying the draft is board-ready.

turns.inner_thought: I'll turn the revised draft quickly and include a brief note so the board pack has what it needs. I should probably make that note cover the implementation points and any supporting material the board would expect if this is truly to be approved for circulation. That keeps us on timeline and closes the gaps I still see.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll circulate a revised draft and a short note this evening so the board pack can move on the expected timeline.
